title: Energetic Costs of Subspace Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Quantum error correction acts as an entropy pump, transferring noise-induced uncertainty from a protected quantum system into syndrome information stored in an auxiliary memory. Repeated operation requires this memory to be cleared which unavoidably contributes to the energetic cost of error correction. Here, we characterise this contribution for subspace quantum error-correcting codes and identify how it depends on the joint structure of the code, the noise, and the representation of the retained syndrome information. Starting from the Knill-Laflamme conditions, we construct an effective syndrome state whose von Neumann entropy sets a lower bound on the ideal work required to maintain a reusable syndrome register. Projective syndrome readout generally generates additional entropy, and we quantify the resulting gap through measurement inefficiency. We then specialise to stabiliser codes under independent local Pauli noise and analyse two classical levels of syndrome representation. At the level of abstract error labels, degeneracies among single-qubit errors reduce the leading-order entropy of processed recovery labels. At the parity-check level, lower-weight checks reduce the marginal entropy generated by individual measurement outcomes in the low-noise regime. We identify the additional burden associated with retaining and separately erasing these outcomes as a bit-level inefficiency, and illustrate both costs for the five-qubit, Steane, generalised Shor, and rotated surface codes. Our results establish a hierarchy of syndrome-memory energetic costs and identify the code, noise, and measurement structures that control the ideal thermodynamic burden of subspace quantum error correction.
summary: This paper develops a detailed thermodynamic analysis of quantum error correction, treating the syndrome memory reset as an entropy-driven energy cost. By analyzing different levels of syndrome information (from abstract labels to raw bits), it quantifies the minimum work required to maintain a reusable syndrome register. The findings establish a clear hierarchy of energetic overheads that dictate the feasibility and efficiency of fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper characterizes the unavoidable energetic cost associated with clearing the syndrome memory in quantum error correction (QEC).
main_result: It establishes a hierarchy of syndrome-memory energetic costs, showing that the cost depends critically on the joint structure of the code, the noise model, and the specific measurement/syndrome representation used.
method: The analysis uses theoretical bounds derived from the Knill-Laflamme conditions and quantifies entropy production, comparing the ideal von Neumann entropy bound against the entropy generated by physical measurement processes.
model_or_system: The focus is on subspace quantum error-correcting codes, specifically analyzing stabiliser codes under independent local Pauli noise. The system involves an auxiliary syndrome memory register that must be reset after each error correction cycle.
key_observables: Energetic cost ($\Delta W_{synd}$), Von Neumann entropy ($S_{vN}(\sigma)$), Shannon entropy of the syndrome distribution ($H[D_V(\sigma)]$), and various entropy measures related to syndrome representation (e.g., abstract label entropy, parity-check entropy).
important_parameters: Code distance ($d$), noise type (independent local Pauli noise), and the level of syndrome representation (abstract labels vs. parity-check bits).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the energetic cost of retaining and separately erasing syndrome outcomes must be accounted for, contrasting the ideal reversible erasure with physical measurement inefficiencies.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates different potential sources of energetic costs in a single round of repetition code, highlighting the syndrome-related cost ($\Delta W_{synd}$) as the primary focus.
paper_structure: The paper develops the analysis in layers: starting from abstract KL conditions, specializing to stabiliser codes under Pauli noise, and finally analyzing the cost at the physical bit-level of syndrome recording and erasure.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous thermodynamic quantification of overheads in quantum computation, directly linking fundamental physical principles (Landauer's principle) to the practical engineering constraints of fault-tolerant quantum hardware.
